claim: pyControl is a system of open-source hardware and software for controlling behavioural experiments.
source: To these ends, we developed pyControl, a system of open-source hardware and software for controlling behavioural experiments comprising a simple yet flexible Python-based syntax for specifying tasks as extended state machines, hardware modules for building behavioural setups, and a graphical user interface designed for efficiently running high-throughput experiments on many setups in parallel, all with extensive online documentation.

evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract describing the system's features.

claim: pyControl tasks are implemented as state machines.
source: pyControl tasks are implemented as state machines, the basic elements of which are states and events.

source: At any given time, the task is in one of the states, and the current state determines how the task responds to events.
evidence: This is stated in the Task definition syntax section.

claim: Events may be generated externally, for example, by the subject's actions, or internally by timers.
source: Events may be generated externally, for example, by the subject's actions, or internally by timers.
evidence: This is stated in the Task definition syntax section.

claim: Whenever an event occurs, the state behaviour function for the current state is called with the event name as an argument.
source: Whenever an event occurs, the state behaviour function for the current state is called with the event name as an argument.

claim: Special events called entry and exit occur when a state is entered and exited allowing actions to be performed on state transitions.
source: Special events called entry and exit occur when a state is entered and exited allowing actions to be performed on state transitions.

claim: Any valid MicroPython code can be placed in a state behaviour function.

claim: pyControl tasks are not strict finite state machines, but rather extended state machines in which variables and arbitrary code can also determine behaviour.

source: The pyControl framework consists of approximately 1000 lines of Python code.

claim: Hardware inputs and elapsing timers place events in a queue where they await processing by the state machine.
source: Hardware inputs and elapsing timers place events in a queue where they await processing by the state machine.

claim: When events are processed, they are placed in a data output queue along with any state transitions and user print statements that they generate.
source: When events are processed, they are placed in a data output queue along with any state transitions and user print statements that they generate.
evidence: This is stated in the Framework implementation section and illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The framework design allows different framework update processes to be prioritised by urgency, ensuring the framework responds at low latency even under heavy load.
source: This design allows different framework update processes to be prioritised by urgency, rather than by the order in which they become necessary, ensuring the framework responds at low latency even under heavy load (see validation experiments below).

claim: Top priority is given to processing hardware interrupts.
source: Top priority is given to processing hardware interrupts, secondary priority to passing events from the event queue to the state machine and processing their consequences, lowest priority to sending and receiving data from the computer.
evidence: This is stated in the Framework implementation section and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Digital inputs are detected by hardware interrupts and can be configured to generate separate framework events on rising and/or falling edges.

claim: The breakout board interfaces a pyboard microcontroller with a set of behaviour ports used to connect devices.
source: The breakout board interfaces a pyboard microcontroller (an Arm Cortex M4 running at 168 MHz with 192 KB RAM) with a set of behaviour ports used to connect devices that make up behavioural setups, and BNC connectors, indicator LEDs, and user pushbuttons (Figure 3B).

claim: The pyboard microcontroller is an Arm Cortex M4 running at 168 MHz with 192 KB RAM.

claim: Each behaviour port is an RJ45 connector compatible with standard network cables.
source: Each behaviour port is an RJ45 connector (compatible with standard network cables) with power lines (ground, 5 V, 12 V), two digital inputs/output (DIO) lines that are directly connected to microcontroller pins, and two driver lines for switching higher current loads.
evidence: This is stated in the Hardware section.

claim: The driver lines are low-side drivers that can switch currents up to 150 mA at voltages up to 12 V.
source: The driver lines are low-side drivers (i.e. they connect the negative side of the load to ground) that can switch currents up to 150 mA at voltages up to 12 V, with clamp diodes to the 12 V rail to support inductive loads such as solenoids.
evidence: This is stated in the Hardware section.

claim: A variety of devices have been developed that connect to the ports, including nose-pokes, levers, audio boards, rotary encoders, stepper motor drivers, lickometers, and LED drivers.
source: A variety of devices have been developed that connect to the ports, including nose-pokes, levers, audio boards, rotary encoders, stepper motor drivers, lickometers, and LED drivers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Hardware section and shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The limited computational resources of microcontrollers preclude generating complex visual stimuli, making pyControl unsuitable for most visual physiology in its current form.

claim: pyControl implements a simple but robust method for synchronisation between behavioural data and other hardware such as cameras or physiology recordings.
source: For neuroscience applications, straightforward and failsafe synchronisation between behavioural data and other hardware such as cameras or physiology recordings is essential. pyControl implements a simple but robust method for this.

claim: Sync pulses are sent from pyControl to other systems, which each record the pulse times in their own reference frame.

claim: The pulse train has random inter-pulse intervals which ensures a unique match between pulse sequences recorded on each system.
source: The pulse train has random inter-pulse intervals which ensures a unique match between pulse sequences recorded on each system, so it is always possible to identify which pulse corresponds to which even if pulses are missing (e.g. due to forgetting to turn a system on until after the start of a session).
evidence: This is stated in the Hardware section describing the synchronisation method.

claim: In a low load condition, response latency was 556 ± 17 μs (mean ± SD).
source: In a 'low load' condition where the pyboard was not processing other inputs, response latency was 556 ± 17 μs (mean ± SD).
evidence: This is stated in the Framework performance section and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In a high load condition, the response latency was 859 ± 241 μs (mean ± SD).
source: In this high load condition, the response latency was 859 ± 241 μs (mean ± SD), the longest latency recorded was 3.3 ms with 99.6% of latencies < 2 ms.
evidence: This is stated in the Framework performance section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The longest latency recorded in the high load condition was 3.3 ms with 99.6% of latencies < 2 ms.
source: In this high load condition, the response latency was 859 ± 241 μs (mean ± SD), the longest latency recorded was 3.3 ms with 99.6% of latencies < 2 ms.
evidence: This is stated in the Framework performance section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In the low load condition, timing errors were approximately uniformly distributed across 1 ms (mean error –220 μs, SD 282 μs).
source: In the low load condition, timing errors were approximately uniformly distributed across 1 ms (mean error –220 μs, SD 282 μs), as expected given the 1 ms resolution of the pyControl framework clock ticks.
evidence: This is stated in the Framework performance section and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the high load condition, timing variability was only slightly increased (mean –10 μs, SD 353 μs).
source: In the high load condition, timing variability was only slightly increased (mean –10 μs, SD 353 μs), with the largest recorded error 1.9 ms and 99.5% of errors < 1 ms.
evidence: This is stated in the Framework performance section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The largest recorded timing error in the high load condition was 1.9 ms and 99.5% of errors < 1 ms.
source: In the high load condition, timing variability was only slightly increased (mean –10 μs, SD 353 μs), with the largest recorded error 1.9 ms and 99.5% of errors < 1 ms.
evidence: This is stated in the Framework performance section and shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The framework's latency and timing accuracy are sufficient for the great majority of neuroscience applications, even when operating under loads substantially higher than experienced in typical tasks.
source: Overall, these data show that the framework's latency and timing accuracy are sufficient for the great majority of neuroscience applications, even when operating under loads substantially higher than experienced in typical tasks.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the validation experiments.

claim: MicroPython's automatic garbage collection is triggered when needed to free up memory and takes a couple of milliseconds.

source: Normal code execution is paused during garbage collection, though interrupts (used to register external inputs and update the framework clock) run as normal.
evidence: This is stated in the Framework performance section.

claim: pyControl timers that elapse during garbage collection are processed once it has completed.
source: pyControl timers that elapse during garbage collection are processed once it has completed (Figure 5E).

claim: The 5-CSRT is a long-standing and widely used assay for measuring sustained visual attention and motor impulsivity in rodents.
source: The 5-CSRT is a long-standing and widely used assay for measuring sustained visual attention and motor impulsivity in rodents (Carli et al., 1983; Bari et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and supported by citations.

claim: A cohort of eight C57BL/6 mice was trained in the 5-CSRTT using a staged training procedure.
source: To validate the setup, a cohort of eight C57BL/6 mice was trained in the 5-CSRTT using a staged training procedure (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section.

claim: The baseline protocol used a stimulus duration (SD) of 2 s and a 5 s ITI.
source: The baseline protocol reached at the end of training used a stimulus duration (SD) of 2 s and a 5 s ITI from the end of reward consumption to the presentation of the next stimulus.
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section.

claim: In all three attention challenges, the accuracy with which subjects selected the correct port decreased (p<0.05).
source: In all three attention challenges, the accuracy with which subjects selected the correct port – the primary measure of sustained attention – decreased (p<0.05; paired t-tests comparing accuracy under the prior baseline protocol to accuracy under the challenge condition, Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: In the attention challenges, omissions increased (p<0.05, t-test).
source: Also, as expected, omissions (i.e. failures to poke any port in the response window) increased (p<0.05, t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: When impulsivity was challenged by extending the ITI, premature responses increased strongly (p<0.05, t-test).
source: Similarly, when impulsivity was challenged by extending the ITI, to either a 9 s fixed ITI (fITI) or to a pseudo-randomly varied ITI length (vITI), premature responses increased strongly (p<0.05, t-test), while attentional accuracy and omissions did not (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 6D.

claim: 2 mg/kg atomoxetine could reliably reduce premature responding and increase attentional accuracy (p<0.05, paired t-test).
source: Using the 9 s fITI impulsivity challenge, we found that 2 mg/kg atomoxetine could reliably reduce premature responding and increase attentional accuracy (p<0.05, paired t-test comparing performance under vehicle vs. atomoxetine; Figure 6E), consistent with its previously described effect in this rodent task (Navarra et al., 2008; Paterson et al., 2011; Pillidge et al., 2014; Fitzpatrick and Andreasen, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 6E, with citations supporting the consistency with previous findings.

claim: Head-fixed mice used their vibrissae (whiskers) to discriminate the position of a pole moved into the whisker field at one of two different anterior-posterior locations.
source: Head-fixed mice used their vibrissae (whiskers) to discriminate the position of a pole moved into the whisker field at one of two different anterior-posterior locations (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Mice were positioned on a treadmill allowing them to run.
source: Unlike in the original task, mice were positioned on a treadmill allowing them to run.
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section.

claim: 10–20 s running bouts alternated with longer stationary periods were observed.
source: Although running was not required to perform the task, we observed 10–20 s running bouts alternated with longer stationary periods (Figure 7C), in line with previous reports (Ayaz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section, shown in Figure 7C, and supported by a citation.

claim: Subjects reached 75% correct performance within 5–9 days from the first training session.
source: Subjects reached 75% correct performance within 5–9 days from the first training session, at which point, they were trained for at least three further days to make sure that they had reliably learned the task (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Early in training, mice frequently licked prior to and during stimulus presentation, as well as during the response window, on both Go and NoGo trials.
source: Early in training, mice frequently licked prior to and during stimulus presentation, as well as during the response window, on both Go and NoGo trials (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Following learning, licking prior to and during stimulus presentation was greatly reduced, and mice licked robustly during the response window on Go trials and withheld licking on NoGo trials.
source: Following learning, licking prior to and during stimulus presentation was greatly reduced, and mice licked robustly during the response window on Go trials and withheld licking on NoGo trials, performing a high percentage of hit and correct rejection trials (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The social decision-making task is adapted from that developed for rats by Márquez et al., 2015.
source: Our final application example is a maze-based social decision-making task for mice, adapted from that developed for rats by Márquez et al., 2015.
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section with a citation.

claim: In the social decision-making task, a 'focal' animal's choices determine reward delivery for a 'recipient' animal.
source: In this task, a 'focal' animal's choices determine reward delivery for a 'recipient' animal, allowing preference for 'prosocial' vs. 'selfish' choices to be examined.
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section.

claim: During individual training for the focal animal, subjects increased their rate of completing trials over seven training days (repeated measures ANOVA F(6,42) = 12.566, p=0.000004).
source: Under this schedule, subjects increased their rate of completing trials over seven training days (Figure 8C, repeated measures ANOVA F(6,42) = 12.566, p=0.000004) without developing a bias for either side of the maze (p>0.27 for all animals, t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Focal animals did not develop a bias for either side of the maze during individual training (p>0.27 for all animals, t-test).
source: Under this schedule, subjects increased their rate of completing trials over seven training days (Figure 8C, repeated measures ANOVA F(6,42) = 12.566, p=0.000004) without developing a bias for either side of the maze (p>0.27 for all animals, t-test).
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 8C.

claim: During individual training for the recipient animal, the recipient animals developed a strong preference for the active poke over the course of training (repeated measures ANOVA F(12,24) = 3.908, p=0.002).
source: Under this schedule, the recipient animals developed a strong preference for the active poke over the course of training (Figure 8D, right panel, repeated measures ANOVA F(12,24) = 3.908, p=0.002), with approximately 95% of pokes directed to the active side by the end of training.
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: By the end of training, approximately 95% of pokes were directed to the active side for recipient animals.
source: Under this schedule, the recipient animals developed a strong preference for the active poke over the course of training (Figure 8D, right panel, repeated measures ANOVA F(12,24) = 3.908, p=0.002), with approximately 95% of pokes directed to the active side by the end of training.
evidence: This is stated in the Application examples section and shown in Figure 8D.

claim: pyControl can contribute to behavioural neuroscience by making it quicker, easier, and cheaper to implement a wide range of behavioural tasks and run them at scale.
source: pyControl can contribute to behavioural neuroscience in two important ways: first, it makes it quicker, easier, and cheaper to implement a wide range of behavioural tasks and run them at scale.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: pyControl facilitates communication and reproducibility of behavioural experiments because the task definition syntax is highly readable and self-documenting features ensure that the exact task version and parameters used to generate data are automatically stored with the data itself.
source: Second, it facilitates communication and reproducibility of behavioural experiments, both because the task definition syntax is highly readable and because self-documenting features ensure that the exact task version and parameters used to generate data are automatically stored with the data itself.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: In pyControl, user-created task definition code runs directly on a pyboard microcontroller, supported by framework code that determines when user-defined functions are called.
source: The first is that in pyControl user-created task definition code runs directly on a pyboard microcontroller, supported by framework code that determines when user-defined functions are called.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a key design choice.

claim: In Bpod, user code written in either MATLAB or Python is translated into instructions passed to the microcontroller, which itself runs firmware implemented in C++.
source: This contrasts with Bpod, where user code written in either MATLAB (Bpod) or Python (PyBpod) is translated into instructions passed to the microcontroller, which itself runs firmware implemented in the lower-level language C++.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a comparison with Bpod.

claim: Running user Python code directly on the microcontroller avoids separating the task logic into two conceptually distinct levels.
source: Running user Python code directly on the microcontroller avoids separating the task logic into two conceptually distinct levels – flexible code written in a high-level language that runs on the computer, and the more constrained set of operations supported by the microcontroller firmware.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an advantage of pyControl's design.

claim: A disadvantage of running the task entirely on the microcontroller is that microcontroller resources are more limited than a computer.
source: The two principal disadvantages of running the task entirely on the microcontroller are (1) although modern microcontrollers are very capable, their resources are more limited than a computer – which constrains how computationally and memory-intensive task code can be and precludes using modules such as NumPy.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a disadvantage of pyControl's design.

claim: Running the task entirely on the microcontroller precludes lack of access to the computer from task code.
source: (2) Lack of access to the computer from task code, for example, to interact with other programs or display custom plots.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a disadvantage of pyControl's design.

claim: An API is being developed to allow pyControl tasks running on the microcontroller to interact with user code running on the computer.
source: To address these limitations, we are currently developing an application programming interface (API) to allow pyControl tasks running on the microcontroller to interact with user code running on the computer.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a future development.

claim: The pyControl breakout board tries to make connectors as flexible as possible at the cost of not being specialised for particular functions.
source: The two most significant are (1) the pyControl breakout board tries to make connectors (behaviour ports and BNC) as flexible as possible at the cost of not being specialised for particular functions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hardware design difference from Bpod.

claim: Bpod tends to use a given connector for a specific function.
source: Bpod tends to use a given connector for a specific function; for example, it has separate behaviour ports and module ports, with the former designed for controlling a nose-poke, and the latter for UART serial communication with external modules.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a comparison with Bpod's hardware design.

claim: Bpod uses external modules, each with its own microcontroller and C++ firmware, for functions which pyControl implements using the microcontroller on the breakout board.
source: (2) Bpod uses external modules, each with its own microcontroller and C++ firmware, for functions which pyControl implements using the microcontroller on the breakout board, specifically analog input and output, I2C serial communication, and acquiring signal from a rotary encoder.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hardware design difference from Bpod.

claim: These design choices make pyControl hardware simpler and cheaper.
source: These design choices make pyControl hardware simpler and cheaper.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a consequence of design choices.

claim: Purchased commercially, the Bpod state machine costs $765 compared to €250 for the pyControl breakout board.
source: Purchased commercially the Bpod state machine costs $765 compared to €250 for the pyControl breakout board, and Bpod external modules each cost hundreds of dollars.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a price comparison.

claim: Bonsai represents a very different formalism for experiment control that is not based around state machines.
source: Bonsai (Lopes et al., 2015) represents a very different formalism for experiment control that is not based around state machines.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation.

claim: In Bonsai, the user designs a dataflow by arranging and connecting nodes in a graphical interface.
source: Instead, the Bonsai user designs a dataflow by arranging and connecting nodes in a graphical interface, where nodes may represent data sources, processing steps, or outputs.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai can work with a diverse range of data types including video, audio, analog, and digital signals.
source: Bonsai can work with a diverse range of data types including video, audio, analog, and digital signals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai is very powerful, and it is likely that any task implemented in pyControl could also be implemented in Bonsai.
source: Bonsai is very powerful, and it is likely that any task implemented in pyControl could also be implemented in Bonsai.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Bonsai can perform computationally demanding real-time processing on high-dimensional data such as video, which is not supported by pyControl.
source: The reverse is certainly not true as Bonsai can perform computationally demanding real-time processing on high-dimensional data such as video, which is not supported by pyControl.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: pyControl's task definition syntax may be more intuitive for tasks where extended state machines are a natural formalism.
source: (1) pyControl's task definition syntax may be more intuitive for tasks where (extended) state machines are a natural formalism.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a reason to consider pyControl over Bonsai.

claim: pyControl is explicitly designed for efficiently running high-throughput experiments on many setups in parallel.
source: (2) pyControl is explicitly designed for efficiently running high-throughput experiments on many setups in parallel.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a reason to consider pyControl over Bonsai.

claim: pyControl hardware modules can simplify the physical construction of behavioural setups.
source: (3) pyControl hardware modules can simplify the physical construction of behavioural setups.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a reason to consider pyControl over Bonsai.

claim: pyControl and Bonsai are often complementary in practice.
source: In practice, we think the two systems are often complementary; for example, we use Bonsai in our workflow for acquiring and compressing video data from sets of pyControl operant boxes (GitHub; Akam, 2020), and we hope to integrate them more closely in future.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to an example.

claim: pyControl is under active development.
source: pyControl is under active development.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: A home cage training system is being prototyped which integrates a pyControl operant box with a mouse home cage.
source: We are currently prototyping a home cage training system which integrates a pyControl operant box with a mouse home cage via an access control module which allows socially housed animals to individually access the operant box to train themselves with minimal user intervention.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a future development.

claim: Hardware is being developed to enable much larger-scale behavioural setups, such as complex maze environments with up to 68 behaviour ports per setup.
source: We are also developing hardware to enable much larger-scale behavioural setups, such as complex maze environments with up to 68 behaviour ports per setup.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a future development.

claim: pyControl is a user-friendly and flexible tool addressing a commonly encountered use case in behavioural neuroscience.
source: In summary, pyControl is a user-friendly and flexible tool addressing a commonly encountered use case in behavioural neuroscience; defining behavioural tasks as extended state machines, running them efficiently as high-throughput experiments, and communicating task logic to other researchers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary.

claim: Framework performance was characterised using pyboards running MicroPython version 1.13 and pyControl version 1.6.
source: Framework performance was characterised using pyboards running MicroPython version 1.13 and pyControl version 1.6.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Electrical signals used to characterise response latency and timing accuracy were recorded at 50 kHz using a PicoScope 2204A USB oscilloscope.
source: Electrical signals used to characterise response latency and timing accuracy (Figure 5) were recorded at 50 kHz using a PicoScope 2204A USB oscilloscope.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The 5-CSRTT experiment used a cohort of eight male C57BL/6 mice, aged 3–4 months at the beginning of training.
source: The 5-CSRTT experiment used a cohort of eight male C57BL/6 mice, aged 3–4 months at the beginning of training.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Animals were group-housed (2–3 mice per cage) in Type II-Long individually ventilated cages.
source: Animals were group-housed (2–3 mice per cage) in Type II-Long individually ventilated cages (Greenline, Tecniplast, G), enriched with sawdust, sizzle-nest, and cardboard houses (Datesand, UK), and subjected to a 13  hr light/11  hr dark cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Mice were kept under food restriction at 85–95% of their average free-feeding weight.
source: Mice were kept under food restriction at 85–95% of their average free-feeding weight which was measured over 3 days immediately prior to the start of food restriction at the start of the behavioural training.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

source: This experiment was performed in accordance to the German Animal Rights Law (Tierschutzgesetz) 2013 and approved by the Federal Ethical Review Committee (Regierungsprädsidium Tübingen) of Baden-Württemberg.

source: Animal husbandry and experimental procedures were approved and conducted in accordance with the United Kingdom Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986 under project licence P8E8BBDAD and personal licences from the Home Office.

source: 12 male C57BL6/J mice (Charles River, France) were used, aged 3 months at the beginning of the experiment.

source: Animals were group-housed (four animals per cage) and maintained with ad libitum access to food and water in a 12–12 hr reversed light cycle (lights off at 8 am) at the Animal Facility of the Instituto de Neurociencias of Alicante.
